newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish transport panel rejects fairway fee hikes.
newsitem.headline: Finnish transport panel rejects fairway fee hikes.

text.p: A Finnish transport ministry working group on Wednesday rejected a finance ministry plan to raise Finland's maritime fairway fees to make them fully cover the public sector's costs of maintaining the sea channels.
"Demanding full cost coverage on the current basis would unreasonably burden shipping," the working group said in a statement.
The finance ministry has pushed for increases in marine fairway fees to cover 100 percent of the state's channel costs by 1999.

To satisfy those demands, fairway channels would need to be increased over 10 percent in both 1998 and 1999 -- or alternatively raised 23 percent in 1999, a senior transport ministry official told Reuters in early April.
In its report opposing the hikes, the working group suggested devising a new means of calculating the coverage of fairway costs using a lower interest rate and a different depreciation scheme.
The group said that by the new means of calculation, full cost coverage could still be achieved by 1999 without any increases in fairway fees.
"The working group believes, however, that it would be best if maritime fairway fees could gradually be reduced," it said.
It recommended keeping the fairway fee system unchanged, but said that if the fees were raised, the increases should be borne equally by vessels in different size and ice categories.

Fairway fees were raised 20 percent at the beginning of this year, and the fees are expected to bring in revenues of more than 400 million markka this year, which would cover 79 percent of the costs under the current system of caculation.
The finance ministry's representative in the committee registered a dissenting opinion on the report.
In a separate statement, the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT) supported the working group's suggestion that Finland's fairway fees should be reduced.
"The current unreasonable level (of the fees) is ... apparent in the speed at which transit traffic has shifted from Finland to the Baltic countries," TT said.
"Shipping should not be taxed more severely than other forms of transport in the name of cost coverage," TT said.
